title: Module quiz: How models are made (concepts only)

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A new engineer asks which stage of making a Claude model is behind its skill at carrying on any text, and which is behind its polite replies to questions. Which pairing is right?

options.text: Pretraining gave next-word prediction; human-ranked tuning gave helpfulness
options.says: Pretraining teaches continuation, and fine-tuning and feedback training turn the continuer into an assistant (page 2, the stages section).

options.text: Feedback training gave next-word prediction; pretraining gave the helpful manner
options.says: Ruled out because pretraining is where the model starts to "learn to continue text on a very large corpus", so the order is reversed.

options.text: Tuning on curated examples gave both; pretraining only supplied the vocabulary
options.says: Ruled out because the tokenizer "is built before pretraining and fixed afterwards" and pretraining is where the model learns to continue text, so tuning cannot have given that skill.

options.text: Pretraining gave both; a larger corpus is enough to make a raw model obey
options.says: Ruled out because a pretrained model "is not inherently good at answering questions or following instructions", whatever the corpus size.

questions.stem: A localisation lead budgets translation runs by word count, then finds that one paragraph needs noticeably more tokens in one language than in another. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: That language was added by later fine-tuning, which re-cut its text into extra pieces
options.says: Ruled out because the tokenizer is "built before pretraining and fixed afterwards", so later fine-tuning cannot re-cut any text.

options.text: The larger window used for that language forces the text into finer pieces
options.says: Ruled out because "The window is how much text fits per request", and the vocabulary is a separate thing, so the window does not set the piece size.

options.text: Its learned vocabulary stores longer chunks for the script that dominated the corpus
options.says: The vocabulary was learned from a corpus, so a script that was common gets longer pieces and a rarer one splits into more (page 1, what the tokenizer does to your work).

options.text: The translated text simply contains more words, and tokens track words one to one
options.says: Ruled out because a token is not a word: "a Claude token is about 3.5 English characters", and "the exact number can vary depending on the language used".

questions.stem: A reviewer waves through a number in a report because the assistant is described as built to tell the truth. Which reply is the soundest?

options.text: Written principles removed unsupported claims, so a skim of the figure is enough
options.says: Ruled out because the table lists "A guarantee that any statement is true" among the things training does not give.

options.text: Training aims at honesty without a promise, so the figure needs checking
options.says: The glossary frames HHH as how Claude is trained, a goal and a direction, and the first trap says verification is still the user's job.

options.text: The model states high confidence, so asking it to re-check is the control
options.says: Ruled out because "Verification is still the user's job", and a model's own report of high confidence is not a check.

options.text: A prompt can demand truthfulness, so add that line and skip the check
options.says: Ruled out because "an instruction that fights the training may not win", so a prompt cannot make a trained behaviour certain.

origin.section: What training gives, and what it does not

questions.stem: A team is automating four chores. Which one should be done by a deterministic program instead of the model alone?

options.text: Sorting incoming emails by urgency from the message text
options.says: Ruled out because the table lists "Following instructions and a helpful manner", and a model reads message text well.

options.text: Rewriting release notes for a non-technical audience of customers
options.says: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Fluent language, many languages, code", which covers rewording for customers.

options.text: Proposing likely causes for an intermittent failing test
options.says: Ruled out because the table credits training with "Reasoning patterns it can apply to new problems", which covers proposing causes.

options.text: Verifying every product code is exactly eight characters long
options.says: Exact character work is a tokenizer-level weakness, so code should do it (page 1, first trap).
